Met.et:
From Middle High German mëte, from Old High German mëtu, from Proto-West Germanic *medu, from Proto-Germanic *meduz, from Proto-Indo-European *médʰu (“honey, mead”).
Compare Dutch mede, English mead, Danish mjød.

s: a female given name, variant of Margarete, popular in Germany around 1900
meteor (streak of light caused by extraterrestrial matter entering the atmosphere)
Meteor.et: Learned borrowing from Latin meteōrum, from Ancient Greek μετέωρον (metéōron), neuter of μετέωρος (metéōros, “up in the air”).

s: Mit seinen 30 Meter Länge und mitunter mehr als 150 Tonnen Gewicht übertrifft der Blauwal jedes andere Tier auf Erden.
With its length of 30 meters and weight of sometimes more than 150 tons the blue whale surpasses every other animal on Earth.
Das 20. Jahrhundert wird eingeleitet durch den Brand im Pariser Metro im Jahre 1903, wo 90 Tote zu beklagen waren.
The 20th century was ushered in by a fire in the Paris Metro in the year 1903, where 90 fatalities were reported.
Metro.et: Borrowed from French métro, a clipping of métropolitain.

s: such meat, seasoned and eaten raw, usually on bread (a popular snack in Germany)
Mett.et: From Middle Low German met, from Old Saxon meti (“meal, dish”), from Proto-Germanic *matją, whence also Dutch met. Related with Proto-Germanic *matiz, whence English meat.

Metzger.et: From Middle High German metziger, metzigære, variants of metzjer, metzjære, from Old High German meziāri, mezziāri (“butcher”), from Proto-West Germanic *mattjārī. Perhaps influenced by Old High German mezalāri, mezzilāri (“merchant, moneychanger, butcher”), f…

-meter.et: From Ancient Greek μέτρον (métron, “measure, size, distance; moderate amount, proportion”).

s: Metz (the capital city of Moselle department, France)

Metall.et:
Etymology tree
Ancient Greek μέταλλον (métallon)der.
Latin metallumbor.
Middle High German metalle
German Metall
From Middle High German metalle, from Latin metallum (14th century).

Mette.et: From Middle High German mettī, from Old High German mattina, a borrowing of Late Latin mattina from Classical Latin (laudēs) mātūtīnae (“morning (praise)”).

s: method (process by which a task is completed)
method (subroutine or function in object-oriented languages)
Methode.et: Borrowed from Latin methodus f, from Ancient Greek μέθοδος (méthodos).

Meteorologie.et: 17th century, from Ancient Greek μετεωρολογία (meteōrología), in part through French météorologie, equivalent to meteoro- + -logie.

s: Innenpolitik, Sicherheitspolitik – das ist ein Metier, das die Grünen lange Zeit rechts liegen ließen.
Dafür wird sie von den Firmen bezahlt. Das ist so üblich in ihrem Metier: Carlott Bru ist Influencerin.
Methoni (a town in Messinia prefecture, in southwestern Greece)
Methoni (a town in Pieria prefecture, in north-central Greece)
metre gauge. Some tramways and historic trains run on it.

Metonymie.et: From Late Latin metonymia, from Ancient Greek μετωνυμίᾱ (metōnumíā, “change of name”), from μετά (metá, “other”) + ὄνομα (ónoma, “name”).

s: methodology (a collection of methods, practices, procedures and rules used by those who work in some field)
a strongly flavoured German sausage made from raw minced pork, which is preserved by curing and smoking
metal beater, commonly made of steel
metropolis; very large city; city which dominates its surroundings due to its population, administrative power or culture(s)

Metropolis.et: Borrowed from Latin mētropolis, from Ancient Greek μητρόπολις (mētrópolis).

methodisch.et: From Latin methodicus, from Ancient Greek μεθοδικός (methodikós). Morphologically analyzable as Methode (“method”) + -isch.

s: value of the metal in a coin
speculum (metal mirror, especially in a telescope)

Metaphysik.et: From Latin metaphysica, from Medieval Greek μεταφυσική (metaphusikḗ). By surface analysis, meta- + Physik.

a municipality of Upper Austria, Austria

-metrie.et: From Ancient Greek -μετρία (-metría), from μέτρον (métron, “measurement”) + -ίᾱ (-íā, “-y: forming abstract nouns”).

s: Metzian (a person from, or an inhabitant of, Metz)

Sie verliebte sich in alle neuen Prinzen und Prinzessinnen, die mit der kaiserlichen Familie durch Heirat in Verwandtschaft traten; sie verliebte sich in einen Metropoliten, in einen Vikar und in einen Pfarrer; […].
